en: The Treatise on the Clear Gateway to the One Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna (A Brief Record of Names and Numbers from the *Maulī Bhūmi*) Composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Commentary by the Tripitaka Master of Cien Monastery, Kuiji;
supplemented with explanatory remarks by the Śramaṇa Mingyu of Fuzi in Shu.

The term *dà* (great) has the meaning of distinguishing from the small. The term *chéng* (vehicle) derives its name from the sense of "transporting" (the meaning and the name are used interchangeably). *Bǎi* (one hundred) is a number.

*Dharma* refers to mundane and supramundane phenomena. Thus, there are eight mental factors (*citta-dharma*), fifty-one mental concomitants (*caitta*), eleven material forms (*rūpa*), twenty-four non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Therefore, these constitute the "One Hundred Dharmas" of the Mahāyāna.
*Vidyā* (Knowledge) refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) of a Bodhisattva, so called because it can destroy darkness. *Mukha* (Gate) refers to that which opens and leads to...
"Congestion" refers to the treatise (*śāstra*), which is a designation for the selection of essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and natures (*svabhāva*) used to instruct disciples.
Regarding the "Local Section" (*Maulī Bhūmi*): it constitutes one-fifth of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. As for the brief recording of names and numbers:

from among the six hundred and sixty phenomena (*dharma*), the essential points are extracted by taking the titles and numerical categories of these one hundred dharmas. This was done because the Master [Asaṅga] was in haste.
For those who wish to study among humanity, it is essential to know the essentials.

This treatise establishes its title based on that which is elucidated. Within the Master’s commentary on the title, he explains its meaning, as well as its numerical categories and constituent elements.

Each point is as explained above. Regarding the citation from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (the Sanskrit term *yoga* means "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*), which is the title of this treatise), it refers to the fifth part [of that work].

The *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* states: "The body of this treatise consists of five parts in total: first, the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section), which provides a brief and detailed analysis of the meaning of the seventeen stages (*bhūmi*);
second, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Section on Compendium of Determinations), which briefly compiles and determines the [meanings] within the seventeen stages..."
The profound and hidden essential meaning. Third, the Section on Compendium and Explanation (*Saṃgrahavyākhyāna-vibhaṅga*), which briefly compiles the rules for explaining various sūtras.
Fourth, the Section on Synonyms (*Paryāya-saṃgraha-vibhaṅga*), which briefly compiles the distinctions in the names and meanings of all phenomena within the sūtras.

Fifth, the Section on Matters (*Vastu-saṃgraha-vibhaṅga*), which briefly compiles the essential matters and meanings of the Three Piṭakas. Therefore, it is said that the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Local Division) constitutes one of the five divisions of the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
First: Regarding the six hundred and sixty dharmas, the *Mūlabhūmi-vibhaṅga* extensively explains the roots, objects, and consciousnesses, as well as their fundamental and derivative totals.

For instance, regarding the six types of objective phenomena (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*), within the single category of the object of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), there are twenty-five kinds, namely blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth.
Within the single category of the object of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*), there are twelve kinds, namely those that are agreeable and those that are disagreeable.
Regarding the single object of odor (*gandha-āyatana*), there are six kinds, namely: pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and so forth.

Regarding the single object of taste (*rasa-āyatana*), there are twelve kinds, namely: bitter, sour, salty, bland, and so forth. Regarding the single object of tangibility (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*), there are twenty-six kinds, namely:

earth, water, fire, wind, lightness, heaviness, and so forth. Regarding the matter (*rūpa*) subsumed under the single sphere of mental objects (*dharma-āyatana*), there are five kinds, namely: the ultimate...
Briefly summarizing the "extreme," "distant," and so forth—based on these six types of objective phenomena (*viṣaya*), one can further expand them into eighty-six categories;
the remaining numbers may be inferred accordingly. Therefore, these one hundred dharmas are called a "concise record. Furthermore, a verse on the one hundred dharmas states:

"Eleven are material dharmas (*rūpadharma*), eight are mental dharmas (*cittadharma*), fifty-one are mental concomitants (*caitta*), and twenty-four are non-associated [conditioned] dharmas (*viprayuktasaṃskāradharma*)."
It is appropriate. The six categories of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) constitute the one hundred dharmas.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the six types of grammatical explanation (*ṣaḍ-vyākhyāna*), it is said: "Mahāyāna" refers to the teaching that expresses [the truth], consisting only of the four factors of sound, name, phrase, and syllable;

therefore, it is inferior. The "one hundred dharmas," however, refer to the phenomena and principles expressed [by that teaching], encompassing all one hundred dharmas; therefore, they are superior. Taking the superior...
Regarding "subordinate" (*hīna*): when the subordinate is used to manifest the superior, it is called "the hundred dharmas of the Mahāyāna," following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis.

Furthermore, the "hundred dharmas" are the objects of cognition; because this refers to the complete number, they are superior. "Luminosity" (*prabhāsvara*) is the wisdom that acts as the subject of cognition; it is merely one dharma among the five specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*). Therefore, it is subordinate.
When the subordinate is brought into relation with the superior, and the superior is used to manifest the subordinate, it is called "the [luminosity] of the hundred dharmas."

"Clarification" (*vidyā*) is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound). Furthermore, "clarification" is the subjective cognition, which—being the wisdom (*prajñā*) among the five particular mental states—is inferior.

"Gates" (*mukha*) are the objects of cognition, as they collectively refer to all one hundred dharmas and are thus superior. By taking the superior with respect to the inferior, and using the inferior to manifest the superior, it is called the "gates of clarification" (*vidyāmukha*), which is an *upapada-samāsa* (tatpuruṣa compound).
Furthermore, "gates" refer to the phenomena and principles that are explained; since they point comprehensively to the one hundred dharmas, they are superior.
A "treatise" (*śāstra*) is a teaching that expresses [meaning]; it is inferior because it consists merely of sounds, names, phrases, and syllables.

Taking the inferior in light of the superior, and using the superior to reveal the inferior, the term "Gate of the Treatise" (*śāstra-mukha*) is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound). Furthermore, the "treatise" constitutes the essence, which consists of sounds, names, phrases, and syllables;
the "gate" constitutes the function, which is the capacity for non-obstruction within the treatise. Thus, taking the essence in light of the function, the function is subsumed back into the essence.

Regarding "the essence" (*tǐ*) and "the treatise" (*lùn*): when "the treatise" is the essence, it is a *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound. Furthermore, if the treatise is the essence, it refers to the four factors of sound, name, phrase, and syllable;

"Mahāyāna" constitutes its function. Since this treatise possesses two meanings within its essence—namely, the distinction from the Hīnayāna and the act of transporting [beings]—it is called "Mahāyāna.
By taking the essence through its function and subsuming the function back into the essence, one says "Mahāyāna is the treatise," which is a *dharmadhāraya* compound.

Furthermore, the Mahāyāna’s general teachings on principle, practice, and fruition are superior because they are that which is explained; the treatises are inferior because they are merely the means of explanation.

By subordinating the inferior to the superior and using the superior to manifest the inferior, it is called a "Mahāyāna treatise" (*mahāyāna-śāstra*), following the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis.

Furthermore, the six characters beginning with "Great" (Mahāyāna) are superior because they are the objects to be explained (*vācya*); the treatise (*śāstra*) is inferior because it is merely the teaching that explains (*vācaka*).
Taking the inferior in relation to the superior, and using the superior to clarify the inferior, it is called the *Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna*.

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound). It may also be termed a *sahitaka-adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive locative determinative). Furthermore, the five characters beginning with "Mahāyāna" apply to all one hundred dharmas; as they belong to the objects to be explained, they are superior.
The two characters "Mén-lùn" (Gate-Treatise) are inferior because they are the means of expression (*vyañjana*), whereas [the subject matter] is superior.

Taking the inferior in relation to the superior, and using the superior to manifest the inferior, it is called the *Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*. This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).

Furthermore, "Mahāyāna" is the essence of the teaching as the means of expression, while "Gate-Treatise" is its function; within this essence of the teaching, there is the marvelous intent for awakening and entry.

It is called a *śāstra* (treatise) because it opens the gates of meaning (*artha-mukha*), definitively discerns essential nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-svabhāva-viniścaya*), instructs disciples, and functions to eliminate evil and produce goodness.
Taking its essence through its function and subsuming its function back into its essence, it is termed the *Mahāyāna-mukha-śāstra*. This is an example of the *dharmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
(The ten types of compounds are hereby concluded.)

Commentary: Regarding this, ten types of interpretation are made based on the subject matter. There are two *śeṣa* (dependent) compounds, five *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds, and three *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compounds.

Within the first two interpretations, since the two characters "hundred dharmas" (*śata-dharma*) are included, they should also be understood as *saṃkhyā-viśiṣṭa-śeṣa* (dependent with a numeral) and *saṃkhyā-viśiṣṭa-tatpuruṣa* (possessive with a numeral).
Generally, what is called *śeṣa* takes that which is inferior as the prior member and that which is superior as the subsequent member. Generally, what is called... [text ends]
Master: In the previous case, the superior was taken as the subject and the inferior as the predicate; or rather, the superior as the function and the inferior as the essence.
Generally speaking, a "function-essence" (*dharmadhāra*) compound takes the superior function as identical with the inferior essence.

Now, this final "function-essence" compound takes the superior essence as identical with the inferior function, which seems to deviate from the formal rule. Previously, the word "treatise" (*śāstra*) was taken as the essence and "Mahāyāna" as the function; now—
Taking the Mahāyāna as its essence and the treatise’s terminology as its function, it leaves the student at a loss as to where to begin.

Furthermore, within the rules for the six types of *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) and *dvandva* (copulative) compounds, the *ālayavijñāna* (store-consciousness) is treated as a *karmadhāraya* (appositional compound). Here, "store" (*ālaya*) is the function and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the essence;

thus, the essence is placed below while the function is placed above. Moreover, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the two truths (*satya-dvaya*) are also treated as *karmadhārayas* with numerical suffixes (*bahuvrīhi*). It is also...
The five characters and two characters serve as the function (*yòng*), while the characters *yùn* (aggregate) and *dì* (truth) constitute the essence (*tǐ*).
Thus, the essence is situated below and the function above. Although essence and function may interchange their positions, one should not seem to violate the established ritual form (*fǎshì*).
Those of like mind should examine this in detail.
Commentary: As for Bodhisattva Vasubandhu: in the country of Puruṣapura (translated here as "Country of Men") in Northern India, there was a state preceptor who was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan.
He had three sons, all named Vasubandhu (translated here as "Heavenly Kin"), who were descendants of the divine king Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Śakra. Although they were the same...
He had one formal name and another sobriquet. The eldest was named Aśvaghosa, which means "Unattached" (Asaṅga);
he possessed the spiritual faculties of a Bodhisattva. The youngest son had the specific name Bhāranidatta, which means "Mother's Son";
for *bhāranī* means "mother" and *datta* means "son" or "child. The middle son was profoundly learned and widely erudite, having mastered all the classical scriptures.
His divine talent was brilliant and refined; his observance of the precepts was pure and white, such that he had no equal.
His brothers all possessed distinct titles, so the Master was simply named Vasubandhu to avoid confusion.
Relying upon the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, he extensively composed various treatises to explain the Mahāyāna, elucidating the teaching of the Middle Way which is neither empty nor existent.
Appendix: The *Pusadupandou zhuan* (Biography of Vasubandhu) states that King Viśvānara was the younger brother of Śakra.
Śakra dispatched him to be born in Jambudvīpa to act as king for the purpose of subduing the Asuras.
The Asuras had a sister named Mingfei (Vidyutprabhā), who possessed great beauty. When the king saw her, he immediately took her as his wife. The Asura asked, saying: "How..."
"Why have you taken my sister as your wife? The Heavenly King replied, "I am a man without a wife;
your sister is a young maiden without a husband. It was only right that we should take her; why do you express such resentment? The Asura said, "What ability do you possess?"
He claimed for himself the title of "Great Man" (*mahāpuruṣa*). If he were truly a Great Man, he would surely be victorious in battle.

The Heavenly King said, "Let us decide this between ourselves," and they each took up their weapons and began hacking and stabbing one another. The gods possessed bodies of Nārāyaṇa; thus, the weapons could not pierce them.
When the gods hacked at the heads, hands, and limbs of the asuras, these parts would break off and immediately regenerate. From dawn until dusk, they continued hacking and stabbing the asuras.
Rāhu had no sign of death; as his celestial power gradually waned, he grew increasingly exhausted. When night fell, the Asura’s strength became even more powerful and superior.
Fearing that her husband might be defeated, the consort took an *utpala* flower, split it into two pieces, and threw one piece on each side.
She moved back and forth between them. The Deva understood her intention and immediately struck down the Asura’s body.
It was divided into two parts, each cast to one side. The Heavenly King passed through the middle, going and returning; because of this, he lost his life.
The gods dwell in this land to manifest the prowess of a great man (*puruṣa*); for this reason, it is named the Land of Great Men (*Puruṣabhūmi*).
As for the *brāhmaṇa*, this is translated as "Pure Conduct. Those who dwell in seclusion and maintain pure integrity are one of the four castes.
Kauśika is originally the clan name of Śakra; thus it is said he is a younger brother of Śakra and a descendant of King Viṣṇu.

As for the term "Unattached" (Asaṅga), it was derived from his realization of the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); because emptiness has nothing to which one can be attached, he was given this name.
Regarding his extensive composition of various treatises: the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu initially studied the Hīnayāna and disparaged the Mahāyāna teachings.
Later, he returned to the Mahāyāna and extensively composed various treatises to praise the Mahāyāna, thereby clearing away his previous faults.

Regarding the statement "neither empty nor existent": it merely negates the existence of external objects; "consciousness" (vijñapti) distinguishes itself from the emptiness of the mind. Thus, it is said to be "neither empty nor existent," revealing that *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only) constitutes the Middle Way.
This is because the Hīnayāna adheres to the existence of objects while holding the mind to be empty; the Mahāyāna establishes *vijñaptimātratā* to refute this.

*Annotation:* "As the World-Honored One said" originally refers to the Buddha’s teaching; this serves as the proponent's primary basis for the authority from which the Dharma originates.

Regarding the phrase "all phenomena are equal" (*sarva-dharma-samatā*): this serves as a general heading for the hundred dharmas and the two types of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which constitute the central thesis of this treatise.

This is the structural framework of the entire work. If one investigates its central tenets, they encompass the shallow and deep teachings of the holy scriptures throughout the generations, arranged in sequence and divided into eight schools.

The first is the school that maintains the existence of both self and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ubhaya-satya-vāda*). This school subsumes the doctrines of twenty of the five groups of schools (*nikāya*).
These refer to the Vātsīputrīya, Dharmottarīya, Bhadrayānīya, Saṃmitīya, and Mahīśāsaka schools;

alternatively, they may also include a portion of the fundamental tenets of the Sautrāntika school. These two positions—that phenomena exist and that the self does not—comprise three schools in their entirety.
These are the Sarvāstivāda, the Haimavata, and the Bahuśrutīya, further including one portion of the tenets of the Mahīśāsaka;
these constitute the three schools that maintain the doctrine that dharmas have no past or future, encompassing seven complete sects.
Namely: the Mahāsāṃghika, the Kaukkuṭika, the Caityaśaila, the Aparāntaka, the Uttaraśaila, the Dharmaguptaka, and the Kāśyapīya.

Furthermore, it incorporates a portion of the fundamental tenets of the Mahīśāsaka school. The fourth is the school that maintains that the four manifest activities (*prātihārya*) are both provisional and real;
this encompasses the entire Sarvāstivāda-vibhajyavāda school and a portion of the Sautrāntika school. These four schools above belong exclusively to the Hīnayāna.

The fifth is the school that maintains that conventional reality is false while ultimate reality is true; this is the Lokottaravāda school. The sixth is the school that maintains that all phenomena are merely names; this is the Ekavyāvahārika school.
[Schools: These two [schools] are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Seventh is the School of Ultimate Emptiness; eighth is the School of the Perfectly Real in Accordance with Reason.

He received a miraculous white parasol, and his transformative influence harmonized both humans and spirits.
At that time, the Great Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma was first split (the term "split" meaning "divided").

This was due to four groups—the Nāgas, the Elephants, the Learned, and the Venerable Ones—who, while discussing together impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, disagreed on five points.

Therefore, following faith, one speaks of exertion. While "exertion" (*vīrya*) is synonymous with "diligence" (*pradadhāti*), diligence can pertain to all three moral natures (*trividha-svabhāva*), whereas diligence as a factor of enlightenment (*vīrya-sambodhy-aṅga*) is subsumed solely under the wholesome nature (*kuśala-svabhāva*).
Regarding the establishment of the basis: it means that the faculty (*indriya*) is established in dependence upon diligence, and equanimity (*upekṣā*)... [is established].
The three [roots] are established based on four factors. Since they ought to be explained together according to principle, diligence is taught only after the three roots.
